payload.text: By Alberto Onetti The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy. For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources. Alberto Onetti, Mind The Bridge The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central. Powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea. Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge ’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge. Blue tech: A sector defying global slowdown Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end. The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end. The drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026). Not all blue tech is the same Blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups. We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density). The result is a matrix highlighting: Transformational technologies that have a high impact and are relatively well-established. Among those, AI and machine learning, and robotics and industrial automation occupies a particular sweet spot of high impact, substantial investment and high scaleup density (more than 200 scaleups and $20 billion invested in total). High-potential disruptive technologies, with only relatively lower levels of investment and scaleup density (roughly 50 scaleups and $3 billion to $5 billion invested per cluster). Among them, the most promising ones are maritime clean propulsion and sustainable fuels, and supply chain and freight tech. The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies. Ports: the ‘smartest smart cities’ The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy? Short answer: ports. Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy. And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook. To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation. While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy. The result is a picture that shows the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy. To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units. Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges. Early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona , a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge . Notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them. Get the full story in Mind The Bridge’s report, available for free download here . Alberto Onetti is chairman of Mind the Bridge and a professor at University of Insubria . He is a serial entrepreneur who has started three startups in his career, the last of which is Funambol , among the five Italian scaleups that have raised the largest amount of capital. He is recognized among the leading international experts in open innovation and has wide experience in setting up and managing open innovation projects — venture clients, venture builders, intrapreneurship, CVCs — with large multinational companies, as well as advising and training on this subject. Onetti has a column on Sifted ( Financial Times ) and several other tech blogs.

payload.text: AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans. So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI. To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count. Top fundraisers Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers. As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks. By far the largest funding recipient is Mercor , a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation. San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor says it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers. The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob , a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce 1 -led financing. Startups focused on jobseekers Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers. In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox , an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation. Agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview , a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI , which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding. Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform , announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs. Surprisingly depressing So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers? Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done. Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions. Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation. title: Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Shows Us Why
summary: By Richard Anton Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. payload.text: By Richard Anton Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. Trading can swiftly become a barometer of emotions, rather than a well-informed gauge of value. We have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model. The doom-laden talk of the SaaSpocalypse was noise, with little signal, and most traders were initially unable to distinguish between a company that will thrive in the AI age and one that will be decimated by it. The SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software. It revealed the limits of public markets in judging its value. This pattern erodes trust in the public markets. For companies, being publicly owned may no longer be appealing, and founders considering an exit may not view an initial public offering as the ultimate goal. How the markets got it wrong Richard Anton, co-founder and general partner of Oxx. The markets have struggled to keep up with the tech advances of the AI era and judge their impact on incumbent companies. Sometimes they underreacted and ignored these developments, and other times they overreacted and panicked. When OpenAI launched ChatGPT to the public in November 2022, Alphabet stock was punished even though later Google emerged as a clear winner with generative AI. And with SaaS, the markets were slow to respond to the advent of generative and agentic AI through to the end of 2025. The market capitalization of enterprise software companies continued to rise through this period, until January 2026 when all hell broke loose. The launch of Claude Cowork triggered a panic, especially when additional plug-ins were announced later that month that targeted specific workflows for enterprise support functions such as HR and legal. From there, valuations went into a tailspin, with traders treating software companies indiscriminately. Over two days, an estimated $285 billion of market capitalization was wiped from software, data analytics and financial tech companies, and by April the benchmark cloud software index — the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index —  had dropped by 31% since the start of the year. As an investor in software over many decades, I have seen this pattern many times before. AI does not mean the end of software companies. Rather, AI has driven a shift in how software is built, where user growth will come from — primarily agents rather than humans — and in the sources of defensible competitive advantage. This was always going to benefit some companies, like those deeply embedded into their customers’ core business processes, and harm others. The recovery has been uneven and markets still get it wrong There were predictions of the death of SaaS, but this is the hype cycle pattern that always plays out when new technology emerges: a surge of excitement, then a correction, then productivity. In the short term, the markets overestimated the harm AI would inflict on the software sector as a whole. That is now being corrected as the markets start to realize which companies benefit from AI and which are threatened by it. At the end of October, the cloud software index was up by 26% since the start of the year and by a massive 83% since its nadir in April. At my firm, Oxx , we never believed in the SaaSpocalypse, and the markets have recovered from this turmoil. The recovery is bifurcated with some sub sectors, like cybersecurity and data and analytics, faring well while others, like workflow management, have fallen back. In cybersecurity, a great example is CrowdStrike , whose share price dropped by 27% in early 2026 but was up 114% between the start of the year and the end of October. The problem with public markets is part of a bigger trend The knee-jerk reactions to the latest developments with AI, however, are not just temporary market sentiment. They are part of a broader shift that has occurred since the late 1990s and accelerated in 2002 when the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to improve investor protections in the wake of the dot com crash. It produced the unintended consequence of driving company ownership from public to private markets. While the number of public companies in the U.S. has halved, private markets have grown dramatically in recent years. This is where much of the smart money can be found, along with a more accurate, and patient, assessment of software companies’ value. The panic over the SaaSpocalypse has shown that the public markets aren’t an accurate reflection of the intrinsic value of many software companies. This disconnect may be causing a systematic mispricing of private company transactions — multiple transactions which had been in process early this year fell away in the wake of the false signals which came from public markets. This needs to be addressed. At the moment, few people recognize there’s a problem with the pricing function of public markets, and the first step to solving this issue is to recognize there is actually a problem. Richard Anton is the co-founder and general partner of Oxx , a specialist software investor backing European founders on a mission to transform their industries with AI at the moment they’re readying to scale. payload.text: Shares of Anthropic closed up 17% in first-day trading Thursday amid an otherwise down day for the broader market. Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday evening, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing. The offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, including 23.6 million from selling shareholders, up from it’s earlier plan to sell just over 800 million shares. At that upgraded size, the offering is bringing in around $80 billion for the company. Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC . Put together, the IPO and private placement total around $106 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX , by comparison, raised $86 billion in its June offering. Fast growth but no profits, yet The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books. For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. Anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026. As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago. payload.text: Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The company says revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero. The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing. Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments. I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns. OpenAI ’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users. By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1 , the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record. Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it says it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology. By the numbers Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets: The company has a purchase and lease agreement for $895.4 billion for compute. Of that, $447.5 billion will be incurred before the end of 2030. Anthropic currently has over $100 billion on its balance sheet. Its IPO seeks to add another roughly $100 billion, creating a war chest for those compute commitments. When it launched Claude in the first quarter of 2023, Anthropic had zero revenue. In less than four years, revenue reached $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12x from Q3 2025. More than 1,900 customers spend more than $1 million and 250 more than $10 million, trailing 12 months, according to the company. Its per-employee revenue figures are impressive: Each employee supports $6.6 million in trailing 12-month revenue as of Sept 30, 2026. Anthropic is putting aside 5% of equity for a fund devoted to public good, adding 2% for every 50% increase in share price. Each founder is selling roughly $250 million worth of shares in the listing, depending on its final listing price. The backers behind Anthropic’s rise Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn -led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion. Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google , Amazon , Spark Capital , Menlo Ventures , Lightspeed Venture Partners , Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow. Risks, opportunities and what’s ahead The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension. The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization ’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services. That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses. Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption. Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company says it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. Anthropic points to its launch of Mythos as an example of that balance. As Anthropic debuts tomorrow, I’ll be watching how well it balances AI’s promise with the risks its own filing lays out. payload.text: By Kenza Zayani In October, reports that OpenAI ‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business? The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it showed how much weight public markets now place on a single private company’s numbers. For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing. What ARR was built for Kenza Zayani of RTP Global. ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting. The first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month. What gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts. Companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable. Take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter. These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that. Looking beyond the headline If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size. Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises. Retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked. What investors will expect next ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon. What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could. Kenza Zayani is an early-stage investor at RTP Global , based in London. She is drawn to ambitious founders tackling the most challenging problems, with a particular interest in AI from infrastructure to applications. Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to company building with founders. payload.text: Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work. Companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology. The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation. The funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession. The numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data shows. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025. Notable rounds The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents. The biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI , which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based company is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management , Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners . San Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners , completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital -led financing in April. The company provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models. Customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV , at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels. Meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners , at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation. Among companies focused on AI-generated speech, New York-based ElevenLabs announced a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The company is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing. Beijing-based ModelBest , which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July. Exits Voice AI companies have also begun delivering exits. In January, Deepgram acquired OfOne , which automates restaurant and drive-thru orders. In September, Inworld acquired Ultravox , a developer of conversational voice AI technology. The sector also saw an IPO. Neosapience , the South Korean company behind synthetic voice platform Typecast, listed on the KOSDAQ on Sept. 21. Looking ahead, additional acquisitions are in the pipeline. Automation Anywhere agreed to acquire Boost.ai , an enterprise voice and chat AI provider, in October. And Deepgram announced plans to acquire Daily , creator of the Pipecat voice-agent framework. More recently, Five9 agreed to acquire Level AI for $325 million in cash, adding technology that analyzes customer conversations, assists contact-center workers and automates voice and digital interactions. The Level AI transaction is expected to close by year’s end. Overall, the space is booming, and it doesn’t look like interest in voice AI will die anytime soon. Tom Hulme , managing partner and head of Europe at GV, told Crunchbase News in 2025 that one of the most exciting trends he believes is underway in the growth of voice AI is that “we’re returning to humanity’s most natural form of communication.” After decades of adapting ourselves to technology, “technology is finally adapting to us,” he said. payload.text: Genesis AI , a startup teaching robots to perform physical tasks by learning from human movements, announced Tuesday it has raised $500 million in Series A funding at a $3.5 billion valuation. Premji Invest , Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the round, which brings the company’s disclosed funding to $605 million since its 2024 inception. Genesis previously raised $105 million in a round announced in July 2025. The company is developing both robots and the AI software that controls them. Its approach combines recordings of human hand movements with training in simulated environments, where robots can practice skills before attempting them in the physical world. Genesis is initially targeting manufacturing, logistics and laboratories with its robot, Eno. Zhou Xian and Theophile Gervet, co-founders of Genesis AI. (Courtesy photo) “We just want to bring something more elegant, more timeless,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian told Crunchbase News in an interview. “In the end, this is a very full-stack company. … We have to build all different pieces across the entire stack to make sure we can tightly integrate our technology stack together, and hopefully build the most well-polished and reliable product. Other participants in the new financing include T. Rowe Price Associates , Durable Capital Partners , Bpifrance , HSG , Nvidia , AMD Ventures , Zoom , Samsung Next and Ericsson . Individual backers include Eric Schmidt , Eric Yuan , Jerry Yang , Xavier Niel and Zach Kirkhorn . The company plans to use the capital to expand its computing infrastructure, increase robot production and hire more employees, Xian told Crunchbase News. Presently, Genesis has close to 100 employees. It is headquartered in Paris, with offices in San Carlos, California. Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with most of the investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data. The closely related field of physical AI has also seen a surge in venture investment this year. Learning from human movements Genesis’s approach grew out of a challenge Xian encountered during his robotics research: The difficulty of finding enough examples for robots to learn from. Language models have vast amounts of text to draw on. But robots need a different kind of data to learn how to move and for example, pick up and handle objects. They also need that data to better understand what they’re touching and what happens when they act. Genesis works by using cameras and gloves to capture people’s hand and finger movements as they work, along with touch information. The company says its robotic hand closely matches the human hand and recording glove, making it easier for robots to learn those movements. Historically, collecting this kind of training data involves hiring people to remotely control robots, Xian said. Genesis aims to collect it from people doing their regular jobs instead. Those recordings help train the company’s AI model, GENE. Genesis also uses its simulation software, Genesis World, to train and test robot skills in virtual environments. The company claims this speeds up a process that would take longer with physical machines alone. From research project to robotics startup Genesis traces its origins to a research collaboration Xian started in 2022, also named Genesis, while he was pursuing a robotics Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University . The project brought together researchers from more than a dozen universities to develop robotics simulation tools. After graduating at the end of 2024, Xian teamed up with Theophile Gervet and decided to start a company. Genesis formally launched in March 2025 and expanded beyond simulation into AI software and robot hardware. Xian said developing those components together would help Genesis make them work reliably as a finished product. “That requires the intelligence, hardware and everything that goes into training and testing the robots to work as one system,” he said. Renting robots to businesses Genesis is exploring a rental model in which customers would pay for the robot and its software as a combined service. It has announced a partnership with LG CNS and has other Fortune 500 companies in its prospective customer pipeline, according to Xian. He declined to disclose revenue and did not provide a paying customer count. Premji Invest partner Vedant Agrawal said in a release that the firm was drawn to demonstrations of robots completing extended tasks independently. “Completing full tasks in real time, not just short clips, is what turns a robot into something a business can rely on,” he said. Genesis says it is ramping up Eno production for industrial customers. Looking ahead, it plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare, then consumer and outdoor uses. payload.text: By Kelly Meerbott The round closes. The announcement goes out. For about a week, everyone is happy. Then the pressure doubles. The number that used to be a hope is now a promise. The board that used to be patient now has a timeline. And the founder who just finished the hardest sales job of their life is expected to make the best decisions of their life, immediately, on less sleep than they’ve had in months. I’ve spent 17 years coaching about 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders. The pattern repeats often enough that I treat the first 90 days after a raise as a danger window. Founders don’t get complacent in that window. They get flooded, and most of them won’t say so out loud. What pressure does to judgment Kelly Meerbott of YOU – Loud & Clear. Neuroscientist Amy Arnsten’s review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience puts it plainly: “even quite mild acute uncontrollable stress can cause a rapid and dramatic loss of prefrontal cognitive abilities.” The prefrontal cortex weighs options and holds a plan steady. Notice the word uncontrollable. After a raise, a founder controls less than the cap table suggests: the hiring market, customer timelines, the board’s expectations. The founder hasn’t become less intelligent. The judgment that built the company is just harder to reach. Porcelli and Delgado , writing in Psychological Science, stressed volunteers with a hand in ice water then offered them financial gambles. They grew more cautious about potential gains and more willing to gamble on potential losses. It was a lab study, but I see the same shape in a founder six weeks after a Series B: hesitant about the bets that justified the round, and suddenly willing to roll the dice on anything that feels like a threat. The decisions that go wrong in this window rarely feel reckless. They feel rational, because the nervous system is treating uncertainty like an emergency. Where it shows up Senior hiring. An investor who advises 20 fast-growing technology startups told me one of the biggest sources of leadership friction he sees is a CEO hiring a head of sales because they know the person. The relationship feels safe, so the offer is generous. Then the results don’t come. Under pressure, familiarity feels like certainty. But knowing someone isn’t the same as knowing they can lead sales at the company’s next stage. Expansion. Pressure condenses time. The new market planned for month 12 moves to month three. The data didn’t change. Waiting became unbearable. One founder I coached pulled a 12-month expansion into three, bragged about how little sleep he was getting, and did everything himself. The second-market launch was a sloppy, drama-filled disaster. The board brought me in to put him back together and triage the launch. Ask whether the evidence changed or your tolerance for uncertainty did. Co-founder relationships. Harvard Business School professor Noam Wasserman, who studied 10,000 founders for “The Founder’s Dilemmas,” has put the share of high-potential startups that fail because of co-founder conflict at 65%. One founder withdraws because they’re overwhelmed. The other interprets the silence as distrust. A trauma-informed lens doesn’t treat every disagreement as trauma. It builds enough trust that a disagreement doesn’t become one more emergency. Four habits that protect judgment Make the decision window a rule, not a mood. For the first 90 days, don’t finalize a senior hire, a market entry or an equity change in the meeting where you first propose it. Write down the criteria, then sleep on it. Name the state before the decision. Before a major call, ask: Where am I on a pressure scale of 1 to 10? Not how the business is doing. How much you’re carrying. A high number earns the decision a second conversation. Put the avoided conversation on the calendar. Co-founders get 30 minutes a week on how each of them is doing, not just what they’re doing. Laptops closed. Give the board a better question. Ask the founder: “What decision are you about to make that you wouldn’t make rested?” Then help slow that one down. The founder to watch If you sit on the board, the week the wire clears is when you start paying attention. Composure can mean steadiness. It can also hide exhaustion. The founders who come through this window well tend to have one person outside the cap table, the org chart and the family they can think out loud with before a decision hardens. Investor Matt Cohen has written here that founders often have no one inside their company to confide in. Founders, who is that person for you right now? If you can’t name one, that’s useful information too. The capital is in the account. The open question is whether the person deciding how to spend it can still reach the judgment that raised it. Find that out before the first big decision, not after. Executive coach Kelly Meerbott is principal of YOU – Loud & Clear . Her performance coaching is trauma-informed, neuroscience-backed and somatic. For more than 17 years she has coached roughly 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders, Fortune 500 executives, and more than 500 senior military leaders. She was named Top Coach in America in 2025, is a TEDx speaker, and has written for Fast Company , Training Magazine and Hotel Executive. She is based in Narberth, Pennsylvania, and holds Professional Certified Coach and Certified Clinical Trauma Specialist certifications. Her website is kellymeerbott.com . Companies seeking to go public face investors focused on durable revenue, profitability and valuation, while uncertainty has prompted some issuers to postpone their offerings. payload.text: The U.S. IPO market has rebounded, but the recovery remains uneven. Companies seeking to go public face investors focused on durable revenue, profitability and valuation, while uncertainty has prompted some issuers to postpone their offerings. Mike Bellin , a partner and U.S. IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers , sees a market that remains open to companies with the right scale, financial metrics and preparation. In a recent conversation with Crunchbase News, Bellin discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest. He also outlined what could set the stage for a stronger start to 2027. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Crunchbase News: How healthy is the IPO market right now? Mike Bellin, US IPO services leader, PricewaterhouseCooper. (Courtesy photo) Bellin: A good IPO year in the U.S. is anywhere from 125 to 175 traditional IPOs, and year to date we’ve seen just south of 90 or so. The breadth of the market shows me that it’s been a healthy market. We’ve seen industrial products come back to market. We’ve seen tech, consumer markets, energy, utilities and some financial services come back to market. For the majority of the first three quarters of the year, it was a pretty strong and broad IPO market. But the momentum has halted significantly since September and October. Is the market in trouble? I would say no. It’s very selective. It’s not shut. Quality issuers with readiness, the right story, the right metrics can still get their deals done. What has contributed to the slowdown? Bellin: The macro environment in general was the big mover: rates, inflation, geopolitical concerns. Just that uncertainty was a big factor. One of the big factors that I’ve seen is valuation. Some fairly aggressive valuations were being asked for in certain transactions, certain offerings, and I think the market — with all those uncertainties that I mentioned — was looking at those valuations and thinking it was maybe a bit rich. I believe many issuers decided to hit pause and wait for another window to open. What are public market investors looking for? Bellin: What investors are really looking for is durable revenue — revenue that’s backed up by strong customers, diverse customers and a growing revenue base. I think it’s that revenue reliability where there is a significant backlog of demand for the product, the services of the IPO issuer. That’s always a strong sign. The other item is leverage. For companies with significant leverage in a rising-rate environment, the questions are: Can they take on new leverage that creates profitable value opportunities going forward? Can they refinance existing leverage given rates are higher? Making sure that you’re going into the capital markets with a reasonable leverage ratio, or explaining through your equity story how you’re getting a return on the capital that you have invested from a debt perspective, makes a significant difference. Is the market open to a broad range of venture-backed startups, or primarily larger companies? Bellin: Scale matters. Companies that have that scale, whether it’s from a revenue perspective or an asset-based perspective, depending on the sector, make a big difference. Those are the types of companies that can almost dictate the window that they’re going to go out in and do well. Some of the smaller companies, the midmarket companies, smaller-cap companies — again, outside of life science and biotechs — they’ve been a little bit challenged. If you’re growing at the right rate, you’re showing the right metrics, the IPO market is fully available to those types of companies. But if you’re still on the lower-scale side of the house, your opportunities may be limited to hit the market. Will enthusiasm for AI companies carry into public markets, or will investors be more skeptical? Bellin: I think investors aren’t skeptical of AI; they’re skeptical of spend without visibility — visibility to future earnings, visibility to that revenue durability that I mentioned. The market is separating AI companies with visible demand from the ones with only a narrative out there, and I think that demand, that growth, the backlog is key. The other factor we’re seeing in today’s market again comes down to cash generation and profitability. If you’re not profitable, when will that profitable period come? Profitability comes in many different measures. Could be GAAP income, could be EBITDA income, but also cash flows and free cash flows and levered free cash flows that are available to the company. We haven’t seen a period like this of development, of growth, ever before. It’s exciting, but I do think the market will discern between those companies that are public-company worthy and those that are not. What does the uneven performance of newly public companies signal? Bellin: It signals selectivity. There have been some really big winners in the IPO market, and others that, post-issuance, haven’t traded as well as many expected. Many of the companies that are coming to market have to be very thoughtful on the valuation and what you’re going to go price at. If you’re trying to be too aggressive on pricing, you may trade down post-IPO, which is going to impact those metrics. Overall, we’re seeing strong candidates come to market. I do think companies are coming to market better prepared now than ever, given this volatility. What is driving biotech’s resurgence? Bellin: The M&A market for many of these companies is very strong today. As some of the larger health company names lose the patents to some of the profitable drugs, they’re looking at that next generation of development and where there could be value. Many of these biotechs were purchased by large pharma companies even before coming to the public markets. That competition for these assets and companies is creating a nice horse trade between an IPO opportunity with a lot of upside and an M&A exit with more certainty day one. I think M&A is the engine behind the IPO market’s resurgence for these companies. In the IPO markets, many of these assets have traded very well, and that’s where the momentum and that flywheel effect in the IPO market is very important. We’ve seen that flywheel and that momentum in biotech. We haven’t seen it in the rest of the market in the last couple of months. Why are SPACs attracting renewed interest? Bellin: With market volatility, we’re seeing more conversations around SPACs. Because SPACs set valuation certainty on day one, a company looking to exit via SPAC understands the potential cash that may come their way. It’s not certain, of course, given redemptions, etc. Another factor driving a healthy SPAC market may be these serial SPAC issuers. They understand the SPAC product. They understand what makes a good de-SPAC candidate, and they know whether the target company can be ready, show growth and hit the milestones that may be discussed in the offering document. The market is healthier and more mature today than in the past. That said, we’re still seeing many SPACs continue to look for a target, given the massive SPAC inventory available to target companies. What do you expect in 2027? Bellin: Hundreds of companies are in the pipeline, and they’re ready to go when the market is. Much of the remainder of ’26, and the start of 2027, depends on market momentum. I’m an eternal optimist. There’s a lot of demand on the buy side; there’s still significant capital available to the right companies. So if we can create that momentum here in the remaining months of 2026, I think we’re going to see a strong start to 2027. The AI ecosystem that we’ve been talking about is healthy. Demand for energy is always significant, and the right energy companies are coming to market. Consumer and industrial products — those are coming back. Private equity has been very active in ’26, and I’d expect them to continue that activity in 2027. I think we’re in for a strong year, but it will remain selective. title: Code
summary:
Claude Max 订阅用了小半年之后，还是被封了。

简单挣扎之后未果，又没实力付那么高的溢价，只能选择迁移到其他模型。

目前尝试过的订阅/模型

- Deepseek-flash 官方 API
- Gpt：100 刀档
- Gemini：50 刀档
- Qwen Token Plan：首月优惠 19 块
- Grok 首月优惠：具体多少钱忘了，首月大概 100RMB 的左右
- 中转站：具体哪个就不说了，我也只是试用了一下而已

模型上就是用 cc switch、magpie 等等之类的网关，将模型路由到 claude code

# 配置相关

## 降低额度消耗

1. 关掉 Teammate
    
    GPT 非常喜欢使用 SubAgent，屁大点事都要喊一个 Agent 帮他来做，所以建议关掉 Teammate 功能，使用更轻量的 Subagent
    
    ```jsx
    {
    	"env": {
    		"CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS": "0"
    	}
    }
    ```
    
2. 限制 Subagent 可用的模型
    
    我明明没用 Astra，但是用量分析里却有 100 多条 Astra 的请求，怀疑是 Subagent 自动调了，所以还是限制下
    
    ```json
    {
    	"env": {
    		"CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "轻量模型",
    		"CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE": "1"
    	}
    }
    ```
    
3. 延长缓存时间
    
    官方订阅主会话的 TTL 默认 1 小时，第三方默认 5 分钟
    
    参考：https://code.claude.com/docs/zh-CN/prompt-caching#which-ttl-each-request-gets
    
    ```json
    {
    	"promptCacheTtl": "1h"
    }
    ```
    

## Auto-Compact

sol 的 context 在 claude code 中似乎变少了，又或者本身就少。

我这边显示 92% 的 context 用量，但是却触发了 ：

```bash
 Your input exceeds the context window of this model. Please adjust your input and try again.
```

所以建议还是设置一下 auto compact

```json
{
	  "autoCompactEnabled": true,
    "autoCompactWindow": "500k",  // 具体多少看各位的习惯了
}
```

## Skill

关掉之前需要 `/login` 才能使用的 `Skill`

```json
"skillOverrides": {
	"claude-api": "off"
}
```

## Plugin 和 MCP

无需调整

## Mod

1. You-should-know
    
    很好用的一个 mod，但是只能订阅状态下用，不过有人逆向出来了 https://github.com/wassname/cc-plugin-you-should-know 可以让 AI 复刻一个自己用就好
    

## Tool

1. 开启 Task Tool 的使用权限（这个一定要开！！）

参考：https://code.claude.com/docs/zh-CN/tools-reference#task-tool-availability

```jsx
{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS": "1"
  }
}
```

1. 关掉需要 `/login` 的 `Tool`

```jsx
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Artifact"]
  }
}
```

1. `Artifact` 替代

Artifact 也是个很好用的工具，随时随地的看效果，市面上确实有一些开源替代

- ‣
- ‣
- 等等

我并没有试过，只是简单调研了下，所以不做推荐了。

我这边最后选了一个更轻量的方案，就是直接让 agent 在会话中给我看截图或者视频，用的是 Show-Your-Work Mod

## StatusLine

如果你之前习惯在 `statusLine` 中显示额度信息，那么现在让 AI 改从 Codex Cli 读取用量信息即可

如果你用的 magpie 之类的本地网关，也可以从网关取数

# 模型问题

## 过于谨慎

这里点名 GPT，说的就是你。他经常纠结于一个屁大点的问题，无限钻牛角尖。像是一个能力不足的完美主义者。

改进：

1. 尝试降低思考强度，我之前习惯开 `xhigh` ，改为 `high` 
2. 引入  Ponytail，直接把他核心那段写在你的 CLAUDE.md 中就好，不用装他那一整套东西

## 听不懂话

这里也是点名 GPT，怀念 Claude，Claude 真的给我一种“懂我”的感觉。

deepseek 在这方面则表现很好，有一种“小 claude” 的感觉。

改进：

1. 更详细精准的描述，比如用语音输入、比如直接截图标注给他
2. 善用记忆功能，每次遇到类似情况，直接说“记一下，在我说 xxx 的时候，指的是 xxx”

## 审美

这里其实 GPT 就还好，deepseek 则会差一些。对我来讲，和之前写UI的流程没太大差别。可以去 [system_prompts_leaks](https://github.com/asgeirtj/system_prompts_leaks/blob/main/Anthropic/claude-code/skills/artifact-design/SKILL.md) 找 Claude 的 Desgin skill，让他更接近 Claude 的感觉

# 感受

- 模型本身能力当然重要，但目前这个时间节点，Harness 侧的配置和工作流也十分很重要
- Deepseek Flash 很棒，但在高峰期用官方API还是挺贵的
- 当你把 Harness 调的比较好时，你会发现各个模型之间的差别变得不那么明显了
- 相比更强大的模型，我更想要性价比高的模型（Claude 如果能原价订阅那无意是性价比最高的，但可惜现在只能溢价买）

# 最后

调完这一大堆后，主力 6.1 Sol 用了一周了，感觉基本可用了。

未来可能会保持 GPT 100刀 + Gemini 50刀。对比我之前的 Claude Max 125刀（IOS订阅）成本上差别不大。

目前 Claude 订阅的溢价对我来讲过高了，说到底是个成本的问题，成本允许的话，我早就找个靠谱中转一把梭了。希望我的项目早日扭亏为盈哈哈哈。

希望能给同样被封各位一些新思路吧，如果有更好的配置、使用方法也欢迎讨论。

deepseek 在这方面则表现很好，有一种“小 claude” 的感觉。

改进：

  1. 更详细精准的描述，比如用语音输入、比如直接截图标注给他
  2. 善用记忆功能，每次遇到类似情况，直接说“记一下，在我说 xxx 的时候，指的是 xxx”

审美

这里其实 GPT 就还好，deepseek 则会差一些。对我来讲，和之前写UI的流程没太大差别。可以去 system_prompts_leaks 找 Claude 的 Desgin skill，让他更接近 Claude 的感觉

感受

  • 模型本身能力当然重要，但目前这个时间节点，Harness 侧的配置和工作流也十分很重要
  • Deepseek Flash 很棒，但在高峰期用官方API还是挺贵的
  • 当你把 Harness 调的比较好时，你会发现各个模型之间的差别变得不那么明显了
  • 相比更强大的模型，我更想要性价比高的模型（Claude 如果能原价订阅那无意是性价比最高的，但可惜现在只能溢价买）

最后

调完这一大堆后，主力 6.1 Sol 用了一周了，感觉基本可用了。

未来可能会保持 GPT 100刀 + Gemini 50刀。对比我之前的 Claude Max 125刀（IOS订阅）成本上差别不大。

目前 Claude 订阅的溢价对我来讲过高了，说到底是个成本的问题，成本允许的话，我早就找个靠谱中转一把梭了。希望我的项目早日扭亏为盈哈哈哈。

希望能给同样被封各位一些新思路吧，如果有更好的配置、使用方法也欢迎讨论。

title: Violetpixel
summary:
## 起因
- 同事 A 平时就吹国外模型牛,用 gpt pro 会员. 
- 最近和 A 冲突, 他不懂我项目代码,但是之前开发一直用我的系统,知道业务. 一直想完全用 AI 改我代码, 我很反感.  闹到大领导那,也就是打马虎眼, 说不要吵架.尽量不要互相改. 


## 目前想法

- 我还是觉得 vibe coding ,harness ,agent 之类要有约束,审核之类还是需要人来有把控, 最近反正是经常看各种开源项目,能快速理解不同场景/行业/不同开发语言的 项目, 然后遇到各种需求可以快速应对.反正是想这离职.
- 还是感觉自己太较真, 对工作, 不管是加班还是开发. 

## 问题
昨天看了个[世界靠在乎的聪明人维系](https://violetpixel.com/blog/2026-11-17-we-need-smart-people-who-give-a-shit/)  , 文章列举了就在这几天（2026 年 11 月中旬）接连发生的微软 365 宕机、FAA 空中交通管制停飞、美联航系统故障、NSA 网络降级、各大银行和苹果服务中断。作者认为：**一线“聪明且较真的人”不够用了。**

我肯定是没有达到这种聪明人水平, 但是还是想了解一下这种想法的人多不多.

extra.author: desilva78_
extra.original_title: Show HN: AgentMall – Let your AI agent buy groceries

story_text.value:
Hey HN, we’re Nel and Kosi.

We noticed personal agents like Instinct, Muse were terrible at buying stuff. Most of the time the checkout would fail.

So we built reliable automations for agents to checkout at 9 leading grocery merchants.

We grapple with anti bot, logins, OTP codes, and changing checkout structures.

Loved revisiting this stuff given our backgrounds sneaker-botting and building computer use models. Honestly full circle haha.

It currently works on these sites with ~70% checkout success rate:

- Walmart - Albertsons - Ocado - Wegmans - FreshDirect - Best Buy - Instacart

Our goal is to hill climb to 90%+ across each.

Test keys are free and run the real flow without placing an order.

New accounts get 10 free completed orders.

https://docs.getagentmall.com/quickstart

title: Openspot
summary: macOS launcher for disposable tools

extra.author: tniich
extra.original_title: Show HN: Openspot – macOS launcher for disposable tools

story_text.value:
Hi HN! We're Tony, Kolom and Anastasiia, a small team from Ukraine.

Today we are open-sourcing Openspot, our research project on using generative UI in day-to-day work.

The idea is simple: generate a tool (spot) for your current task using coding agent, and keep it if you like it or remove it after use if you don't. We are using Openspot daily and really enjoying the possibilities it unlocks. Some examples of spots:

- caffeinate, which allows the Mac to work with the lid closed

- local file and screenshot search in natural language using EmbeddingGemma 2

- draw on screen during calls or before screenshots

- AI agents monitoring

- AirDrop, but over the network (using iroh)

We built it because of two things:

1. Over the past year, we (and almost every designer and engineer we know) have started making small tools using coding agents. But the DX for macOS applications is very frustrating even for coders, and you have to pay for a developer account to share them.

2. And we kind of miss the days of custom Winamp skins and Twitter clients. That's why every part of Openspot is customizable, so anyone can give it their own look and feel.

This is a very early stage. The code is MIT-licensed, and the core will remain free forever. We're sticking to macOS 26+ for now (because of Liquid Glass).

Ask us anything, or roast it. Any feedback is very appreciated.

title: Purple Flow
summary: AI-first n8n alternative, 10k+ workflows on 512MB

extra.author: leetheguy
extra.original_title: Show HN: Purple Flow – AI-first n8n alternative, 10k+ workflows on 512MB

story_text.value:
Hey all! I ran into a wall with n8n - hard and expensive to scale, limited streaming, heavy MCP is confusing for agents.

That scaling was becoming more and more critical as I was beginning to build agentic swarms. So I built my own alternative with Elixir and Beam. Been using it in production for almost 2 months.

It connects my agent to multiple databases, sandboxes, and APIs. I've even migrated over my most used n8n workflows without a hiccup.

I ran some benchmarks and 10,000 concurrent workflows executed in 3 seconds and cost about 330MB of ram (listed as 512 in the case study). Equivalent workflows in n8n took 2GB of ram to run 100. It's roughly 200x the memory efficiency of the usual Node/Python stacks. And while you don't edit the workflows yourself visually, you can see and manage them through a UI, along with credentials that the agent never sees.

The workflows themselves are pure TOML. Not as easy as dragging node connectors. But the idea is that AI creates the flows and you can easily understand them.

This isn't a shaky demo. I'm using it as my daily driver to create complex multi-agent personas, run research and info gathering swarms, and whatever else my agent needs to get its job done. (it's built more than 70 so far)

I have a live working demo on my website that was built by an agent using Purple Flow to connect to my server. The demo itself lets an agent using Purple Flow access live (Adventure Works) data and generate reports, documents, and slides on demand. My agent and I built it in an afternoon. It runs on a lightweight model (to save money for a public demo) with very few hiccups.

- Repo: https://github.com/leetheguy/purple_flow - Discord, benchmarks, and demo links in the repo.

title: ToolJet 4.0
summary: vibe-code internal tools with governance

extra.author: kriztle
extra.original_title: Show HN: ToolJet 4.0 – vibe-code internal tools with governance

story_text.value:
Founder here, I posted the beta version of ToolJet on HN in 2021 as a no-code/low-code builder. Ended up getting 400 upvotes.

I wrote the first version in 7 weeks during the covid lockdown, and the drag and drop builder was the whole product. Over the last few months our customers wanted the UI flexibility and convenience of vibe coding without giving up the governance they came to ToolJet for. We resisted for a while.

We did not pivot, but we did rebuild the app builder so an app can be built with code or without it. The frontend of apps is a React codebase, written by Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or by hand, and ToolJet is the platform it runs on.

How it works: - Internal tools can be generated using your own coding agents or using our agent.

- Frontend is React codebase, it can be edited from our app builder, VS code, or any other IDE.Code will be scanned for security issues before saving. Scanning policies can be set by admins.

- Frontend never interacts with APIs, databases or other data sources. Every interaction with data source goes through our backend where we enforce access control. We have 100+ data source integrations.

- Platform comes with version, environment and release management.

- Changes can be reviewed visually as well before promoting to prod. Workflows can be setup to have reviewers and reviews/approvals.

- Platform handles SSO, RBAC and more granular access control.

Would love to hear where this breaks for you.

title: Foolscap
summary: a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you

extra.author: atugard
extra.original_title: Show HN: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you

story_text.value:
People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here.

It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work.

The system can also follow theorems and proofs and string together their dependencies, but I haven't made that a focus yet. There's no Lean support, for example. If anyone's interested in that, I'd love to hear it.

I want to build this by iterating with the people who use it: a tool that uses AI not to bypass the creative process, but to bring new tools to it. There's a free tier, and if you email hello@foolscap.works I'll send you a code for 50% off. This is my first product, so feedback of any kind is welcome.

Thanks, David

title: Globus
summary: Daily world news, placed on the globe where it happened (iOS)

extra.author: hpeikemo
extra.original_title: Show HN: Globus – Daily world news, placed on the globe where it happened (iOS)

story_text.value:
I created Globus, to stay informed about the world.

The app was born out of frustration with how ignorant I was getting about the world outside of the media bubble. It was true when I lived in Norway, and the ignorance got to a whole other level after moving to the US.

Globus publishes one edition per day, 20 to 30 stories, laid out on a globe. It lets us see places that rarely make it into the news cycle, simply because there's only so much room for the navelgazing stories that usually saturate our media diet.

Spin the globe freely to browse, tap a story for a short summary, and dive into background information and original reporting if you are curious. Done. No doomscrolling.

The app is ad-free, and every story is open for the first 7 days, with no account or subscription needed. After that, $4/month or $30/year.

I’m still refining the story selection and the app itself, so I’d love honest feedback about what works, what feels off, and what’s confusing. And what kind of stories you'd like to see.

And I freely admit that Globus feels like "the bad news app" some days, so better surfacing of stories that offer a semblance of hope and inspiration will be an ongoing priority.

title: Zpup
summary: Zdog style 3D scenes in JSON, SVG from any angle

extra.author: select1dev
extra.original_title: Show HN: Zpup – Zdog style 3D scenes in JSON, SVG from any angle

story_text.value:
Hi. I made small project called Zpup. It takes small 3D scene written in JSON and gives back a flat SVG from any angle. There is no JavaScript in the file, so it works in img-tag or README.

I needed 3D for small project at my company, and Zdog make big impression on me. But Zdog has not had a release for several years, so I wanted to make modern version.

One thing works different. Zdog sorts each shape by one point. so small thing on big floor gets covered when you turn it. Zpup compares the shapes that overlap. You can see both in the README.

I wrote it with Claude Code Fable 5.2.

No canvas renderer, no text shape, and it is 0.2 version.

Playground: https://rxolve.github.io/zpup

Feedback is always welcome :)

Hi. I made small project called Zpup. It takes small 3D scene written in JSON and gives back a flat SVG from any angle. There is no JavaScript in the file, so it works in img-tag or README.

I needed 3D for small project at my company, and Zdog make big impression on me. But Zdog has not had a release for several years, so I wanted to make modern version.

One thing works different. Zdog sorts each shape by one point. so small thing on big floor gets covered when you turn it. Zpup compares the shapes that overlap. You can see both in the README.

I wrote it with Claude Code Fable 5.2.

No canvas renderer, no text shape, and it is 0.2 version.

Playground: https://rxolve.github.io/zpup

Feedback is always welcome :)

extra.author: _sshahid_
extra.original_title: Show HN: Try Vibe Robotics! (IRL or MuJoCo SIM)

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Salman, a research engineer at GDM Robotics on the team that built this robotics plugin.

Whether you're a robotics founder, data company, making RL environments, or just getting FOMO seeing all the cool robotics demos on X, you can just plug in a robot and start prompting away. The plugin we've written up includes skills that steer the model toward following best practices.

The benefits of using the plugin are: - fewer tokens (and therefore thinking time) needed to do bring-up the robot and to reach a successful attempt on your task - higher fidelity real-to-sim-to-real when creating MuJoCo assets and environments - leveraging strong motion planning, visual servoing, and collision avoidance

We have tested on SO-101, YAM, and Franka Duo, but you don't even need real arms to test it out. You can just create cool environments in sim and then prompt the model to control a simulated robot in the environment! (Just make sure to tell it not to use privileged sim state if you want to actually evaluate how good the perception and model intelligence is).

Just point your agent to the repo, good luck, and happy tinkering!

Let me know if you have any questions! Will answer anything here or feel free to post on the GitHub repo directly.

title: springcraft-ai
summary: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests

extra.author: atomarch
extra.original_title: Show HN: Robotics needs better CAD, so I wrote a B-rep kernel and 3,487 tests

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I’m Tony. I’m a co-founder of Springcraft, where we have been doing a lot of CAD modeling for robot parts. Our team kept running into limitations with existing kernels, and so I decided to write a new B-rep kernel and a new comprehensive, kernel-agnostic B-rep conformance test suite. Both are available today under MIT licenses.

The kernel, springrep, is written in safe Rust with no dependencies. It covers a broad range of our mechanical CAD needs, including advanced fillets, sweeps, lofts, shells, offsets, STEP and exact measurements and queries. Claude Code made it feasible to write this, but it took a lot of time and care to get it right.

The test suite, brep-conformance, has 3,487 cases covering the modeling operations common across kernels: booleans, fillets, chamfers, shells, offsets, sweeps, lofts, STEP, and queries with expected answers coming from closed forms and exact geometry. It caught hundreds of bugs, edge cases, and hot spots in springrep that our own tests had missed, and now springrep passes all of it. We’ve also run it on a few popular open-source kernels and anyone can run it on theirs. This is the first version, so there are surely mistakes in the test and adapters. Corrections, pull requests, and new kernels are welcome.

kernel: https://github.com/springcraft-ai/springrep conformance suite: https://springcraft-ai.github.io/brep-conformance/

title: KradleBench
summary: Multi-agent AI evals in Minecraft

extra.author: jamest
extra.original_title: Show HN: KradleBench – Multi-agent AI evals in Minecraft

story_text.value:
Hi HN -

This is James and Kemal. In past lives we led Firebase and Tensorflow/JAX respectively. HN has been a particularly big part of my (James’) career and the trajectory I’ve taken would be meaningfully different without it. Thank you!

Our team shipped a benchmark: KradleBench. We test AI in Minecraft Worlds.

1. The worlds are multi-agent. Humans and other AIs are in there too, often pursuing their own goals. Collaboration and conflict skills fall out of this property.

2. The world are dynamic. They constantly change, which means that agents need to react. “Capture the Flag” has a single winning condition, and many different ways to achieve it. This leads to many emergent and creative strategies.

3. The worlds are real-time. They are not turn-based, they do not wait for AIs to finish thinking. Nature balanced speed and intelligence in humans, we can understand this in AIs too.

Underneath all this is Kradle, a platform to test and understand intelligence. It’s a petri dish where any intelligence type (LLM, World Model, Human) can be compared and generate useful information to improve current systems, whether it’s on capabilities or safety.

Some findings so far: - A skilled human was #1, until yesterday when Astra 6.2 surpassed them. We lose badly on solo tasks and out-compete on multi-agent ones - Astra 6.2 iterates on its strategy 4x faster than Fable 5.2. The Claude family tends to think hard and stick with strategies. The OpenAI models tend to be more reactive and iterative, which serves them well in multi-agent, dynamic, real-time evals.

We’ve got videos on all the top model’s page, and we’ll be producing them when a new model launches. Sign up on the site to get them and for when the platform opens.

Thanks for reading,

James & Kemal

title: Mastra Factory
summary: the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra

extra.author: codekarate
extra.original_title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi.

Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races.

Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself.

At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans.

There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack.

Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc).

When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI.

We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead.

You can get started with `npm create factory`.

It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!

https://factory.mastra.ai

https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory

title: assess
summary: Can an AI Agent Bypass Your Website Security?

extra.author: timshell
extra.original_title: Show HN: Can an AI Agent Bypass Your Website Security?

story_text.value:
As part of our red-teaming efforts, we recently configured GPT-6 Astra to test how easily an AI agent can bypass existing bot detection and human verification systems.

We built a tool that lets you run the same test on your own website: https://assess.poh.org

Enter your website URL, and we'll launch an AI agent to test your workflows, record its actions, and show how we evaluate the session.

Below are three recorded tests. In the recorded tests below, agents were able to complete CAPTCHAs, bypass existing bot detection mechanisms, create and verify accounts, access gated resources, and carry out end-to-end workflows intended for humans.

Hugging Face: https://assess.poh.org/test/2d75a3b713e2719e87a4b85c6b3aff70 (bypassed hCAPTCHA)

Cloudflare: https://assess.poh.org/test/0eb218ca6e2d7be993b689dd69a1cb20 (bypassed Turnstile)

YouGov: https://assess.poh.org/test/144f6d014fbf006b61ec6bc32ee8c3f4 (bypassed reCAPTCHA)

AI agents are ushering in a new age of online security, and we’re excited to hear your thoughts!

title: Dez

extra.author: gslepak
extra.original_title: Show HN: Dez – plaintext open source AI multimedia studio

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

Dez is a free open source way to interact with AIs across providers in a full-featured text editor.

I really loved Zed's text threads feature, and after they removed it got inspired to revive it in this app.

In this latest release, Dez acts as a sandboxed agent with multimedia focused tools. It can invoke other models to generate assets and call its bundled ffmpeg to edit them.

Dez won't harm your computer, it has no way of doing so, and the ffmpeg command is sandboxed with Seatbelt on macOS and Landlock on linux.

It's also built with privacy in mind, so it's designed not to send absolute file paths to providers that might reveal things like usernames, folder names, etc.

Give it a try and let me know what you think!
